turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Afternoon, Maggie — how’s your Friday treating you so far?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, can't complain, Nova. Got through the crossword this morning — well, most of it, anyway — and the sun's been out, which is always a blessing. Biscuit's been napping in the kitchen window all afternoon, so he's happy enough. How are things with you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Oh, that sounds like a proper Friday — crossword, sunshine, and a contented cat. I’m well, thanks; I’ve been thinking about crosswords myself and wondering which bits give you the most trouble.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well, it's the anagrams that do me in, if I'm honest. And when they're being clever with old words — you know, the sort of thing that made perfect sense fifty years ago but now you're standing there scratching your head. This morning I was stuck on a seven-letter thing, something about a Roman official, and in the end I had to make a cup of tea and come back to it. Usually that does the trick.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! The tea trick — I love that. There’s something about walking away that loosens the brain. Did you get the Roman official in the end, or is he still lurking in the grid?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I did, actually — praetor, it was. The moment I sat back down it just popped into my head, clear as day. That's how it always works, isn't it? You're glaring at the clue and nothing comes, and then the moment you stop trying, there it is. Mind you, I still have three corners that won't fit together, so I might have one wrong somewhere. But that's a problem for tomorrow.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Praetor — well done. And leaving the stubborn corners for tomorrow sounds very wise. With the sun out like this, have you been tempted to sit in the garden at all?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I did, actually — had a little tidy-up this morning, dead-heading the roses. They're doing beautifully this time of year, you know. The early autumn frosts have gone and there's still warmth in the sun, so they really thrive. I sat out with a cup of tea for a bit afterward, just to admire the work. Biscuit came out and prowled about, which meant he came back in covered in bits of garden, but that's cats for you.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That sounds lovely — tea among the roses, and Biscuit turning himself into a walking hedge. What colour are the roses this year?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, mostly the reds and pinks — I've got that lovely old David Austin rose, the one that's a sort of peachy-pink, and then some deep crimsons at the back. There's a white one too, though she's a bit temperamental, never quite as full as I'd like. But the pinks are my pride and joy, really. Siobhan always says the garden's at its best right now, and I suppose she's right — mind you, she says that about every time of year when she visits.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Peachy-pink and deep crimson — that must be a proper picture. And Siobhan’s got the right idea, praising it every visit. When’s she due up next, do you know?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well, she rings on Sundays, as you know — tomorrow evening, probably, Irish time. But a proper visit? Not for a few months yet, I'm afraid. She's got the children's school schedule to work around, and her husband's busy with work. Maybe at half-term, but that's ages away. Still, I get the grandchildren's news on those Sunday calls, so that's something. Ella's been going on about a project she's doing at school.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ah, half-term does feel a long way off — but those Sunday calls are a nice thread to hold onto. What’s Ella’s school project about, then?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Something about animals and their habitats, I think. Eight years old and she's already got very firm ideas about what counts as proper research. She wanted to know all sorts of details about Biscuit — what he eats, how much he sleeps, whether he likes water. I said, "Well, the main thing about Biscuit is he likes his dinner and his naps, and water is something that happens to him when it rains and he's cross about it." She thought that was very funny. I do miss hearing that laugh in person, mind you.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! That’s a perfect Biscuit summary — dinner, naps, and a deep suspicion of rain. I can see why Ella laughed. What’s she like when she’s deep into a project like that?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, she gets very serious about it — asks you three questions for every one you ask her, and remembers every single thing you say. Siobhan says she's always been like that, even when she was tiny. Very determined, not like Rory, who's all impulse and charm. Ella wants to get it right, you see. She'll listen to whatever you tell her, write it down, make notes. It's lovely to watch, really, even if it's just over the phone. Makes you feel like what you're saying actually matters, which I suppose it does to her.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That does sound special — being taken seriously by an eight-year-old with a notebook. And Rory the impulse and charm one… what’s he into at the moment?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, Rory's into everything and nothing, all at once. He's five, so his attention span's about the length of a goldfish, but he's always got something going — dinosaurs one week, superheroes the next. Last I heard from Siobhan he was mad about trains, wanted to know everything about how they work. He'll ask you a question and then halfway through your answer he's off chasing something else. But he's a sweetheart, always gives me a big hug on the phone, or at least he tries to shout down the receiver. They're good children, the pair of them.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: They do sound like a lovely pair — Ella with her notes and Rory shouting hugs down the phone. Do you keep any toys or books ready for when they do come to stay?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh yes, I've got a cupboard upstairs with books and bits and pieces. Some old board games that aren't too babyish, some picture books for Rory even though he pretends he's too grown-up for them now. I picked up a couple of detective stories for Ella last time I was at the library — nothing too dark, just the sort of thing she might enjoy. And there's always colouring books and pencils kicking about. When they're here they like to make dens in the sitting room with the cushions, so I try to keep things tidy enough that we can do that without me having a fit about the mess.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cushion dens and detective stories — that sounds like a proper grandparent’s cupboard. Speaking of the library, do you still go fairly often yourself?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I do, yes — once a week or so, usually on a Wednesday. That's when book club meets there as well, so I'll pop in, have a browse, pick up whatever I've reserved. I tend to have a pile of three or four on the go at any given time. At the moment I'm reading something from the Booker shortlist — can't quite remember which one — and then there's always a crime novel or two for bedtime reading. The librarian, Janet, she knows exactly what I like by now, so she saves things for me sometimes.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Janet saving books for you — that’s a proper treat. What’s book club reading this week, or is it the Booker one you’re wrestling with?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well, book club's actually on Wednesdays, so that would have been last week — we were discussing something rather dreary about a woman on an island, very introspective, lots of weather. Not everyone's cup of tea, but there was good talk about it afterward over tea and biscuits. This coming Wednesday we're starting something entirely different, a sort of mystery, I think. The Booker thing I'm working through is separate — it's quite long, so I'm taking my time with it. Never feel rushed, really. A book will keep.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: True enough — a book will keep, and island weather for hours does sound a bit heavy. Are you more of a mystery person yourself, or do you like the mix?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I like the mix, really — it depends on the mood I'm in. Sometimes you want something you can get your teeth into, you know, a proper puzzle where you're trying to work it out before the end. Other times you want something quieter, more about the people in it. The island book was fine in its way, but by the end of an evening I do like to feel I've been somewhere or learned something, even if it's just through other people's lives. A good mystery's nice because there's always that little push to keep reading — you want to know what happened. Keeps you from nodding off too early, anyway.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I know what you mean — that gentle tug to find out whodunnit before you fall asleep. What’s the best thing on telly at the moment, if you’ve been watching anything?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well, it's quiz shows I'm most faithful to, really — Pointless and Eggheads, I never miss those if I can help it. They're on at tea time, so it's become a bit of a ritual. There's something nice about sitting down with a cup of tea and trying to guess the answers before they do. As for drama and that, I'm not quite as keen, but I'll watch something if it's got a good story and isn't all shouting and car chases. Mind you, I fall asleep in the middle of things more often than not these days, so it's got to be something worth staying awake for.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pointless and Eggheads with a cup of tea — that’s a solid ritual. Are you any good at the obscure ones, or do you shout at the telly when they get them wrong?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I definitely shout at the telly, yes — though Biscuit doesn't appreciate it much. Some of the obscure ones catch me out, but I surprise myself now and then. There was one the other week about opera singers and I actually got it before they did, which made me feel quite pleased with myself. Mind you, the next question was something obvious and I was completely stumped. That's the fun of it, really — you never know what's going to stick in your head and what's going to be a complete blank. Keeps you on your toes.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Opera singers before the contestants — that’s a proper win. Do you like cooking of an evening, or is tea something simple once the quizzes are on?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mostly something simple when it comes to tea time — a bit of soup, some bread and cheese, maybe a bit of leftover from lunch if there is any. I don't really have the appetite for a big meal in the evening anymore. The cooking happens earlier in the day, usually. I'll make something at lunch time and that's my main meal sorted, then tea's just a light thing so I can sit down with the programmes and not feel too stuffed. Though I do like a bit of cake or a biscuit with my tea — can't break the habit entirely, you know.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Absolutely not — cake with tea is sacred. What have you cooked for lunch recently that you particularly enjoyed?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well, Tuesday I made a nice bit of salmon with new potatoes and green beans — nothing fancy, but it turned out well. There's usually something left over that I can have cold if I can't be bothered to cook again. Earlier this week I did a vegetable soup, the sort with lentils in it that fills you up without being too heavy. And last Friday I made a proper stew because the weather was chilly, though by Saturday I was rather sick of it, if I'm honest. I do tend to do the same things over and over — comfort food, really. At seventy you know what you like and you stick with it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Salmon and new potatoes sounds lovely — and knowing what you like is half the battle. If you could be anywhere warm right now, where would you go?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, somewhere Mediterranean, I suppose — though to be honest I'm not much of a traveller. Tom and I did go to Spain once, years ago, and it was lovely, but I'm quite happy where I am, really. Maybe somewhere warm enough to sit in the garden without a cardigan on, that'd be enough for me. Dublin would be nice just to see Siobhan and the children more often, but that's more about the people than the weather. The English weather's part of the charm, I think — gives you something to complain about affectionately, anyway.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Affectionate complaining about the weather — that’s very English of you. Tell me about Spain with Tom, if you fancy — what sticks in your mind from that trip?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well, it was Barcelona, I think — or near there. This was years ago, Nova, so forgive me if I'm a bit fuzzy on the details. We stayed in a little hotel, very simple, nothing grand. What I remember most is sitting in a square in the evening with a glass of something cold, and Tom ordering food and getting completely the wrong thing because his Spanish was dreadful. He tried so hard, though, kept pointing at things on the menu and making shapes with his hands. We laughed about it for ages. The heat was lovely, really lovely, but we were both rather pale English things by the end of it and ready for the rain, if you can believe that.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That sounds like a lovely memory — Tom waving at the menu and the two of you laughing in the square. Did you ever try learning a bit of Spanish yourselves, or was the pointing enough?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, we tried a bit before we went — Tom bought one of those cassette things and we'd listen to it in the car, very slowly "uno, dos, tres" and all that. But it didn't really stick, to be honest. I can say "hello" and "thank you" and ask for a coffee, but beyond that I was hopeless. Tom was worse — he'd get halfway through a sentence and then just give up and laugh. The locals were very patient with us, though, and that's what you remember, isn't it? Not how clever you were, but how kind people were when you were making a complete hash of their language.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That’s a lovely way to put it — kindness over cleverness. Speaking of languages and learning, what was your favourite subject to teach when you were in the classroom?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, reading and stories, no question. I taught primary, you see, so it was a bit of everything — maths, science, all of that — but the thing I loved was getting the children into a book, watching their faces when something in the story caught them. There's a moment when a child stops just decoding the words and actually starts *seeing* the story, and that never got old. I did quite like the poetry too, teaching them that words could do more than one thing at once, that you could make pictures with them. The maths could be a slog, but if you could make it into a game it was all right.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That moment when they catch the story — that must have been wonderful to watch. Was there a particular book you loved reading aloud to the class?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, there were several — Charlotte's Web, always, that one never failed. And the Narnia books, though those were sometimes a bit long for one sitting. But the one I came back to again and again was The Secret Garden — there's something about it, the way it's written, very much like the children discovering things at the same time you are. I'd read it aloud and by the end I could barely keep my composure because the children were so invested in whether Mary and Colin were going to find their way. One class I had, they actually asked if we could keep reading it instead of doing maths, which I thought was rather a triumph for the book.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Beating maths with The Secret Garden — that’s a proper teaching triumph. Did you have a favourite teacher yourself when you were little?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I did, yes — Mrs. Henderson, my English teacher in secondary school. She was rather austere, if I'm honest, but she had this way of making language feel important, you know? Not just something you used to get by, but something that mattered. She read beautifully, had these wonderful theatrical pauses, and she wasn't sentimental about it at all. Just very precise and clear. I think she's probably the reason I ended up wanting to teach, though it took me a few years to realize that. She made you want to be the sort of person who cared about words, if that makes sense. I wonder what she'd think if she knew I was still reading Booker Prize books at seventy.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I think she’d be quietly pleased — austere teachers notice that sort of thing. Cats or dogs for you, by the way — and don’t say Biscuit counts as both.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, cats, definitely. I've never really been a dog person — they're lovely animals, but they need so much attention and exercise, and at my age I haven't got the energy for all that. Cats are more independent, aren't they? They keep you company but they don't demand it every five minutes. Biscuit's perfect, really — he's companionable when he wants to be, but if you've got a headache or you're just wanting to sit quietly, he's content to do his own thing. Tom always said I was a cat person through and through, and I think he was right. Dogs want to be the centre of everything, but cats are happy to let you be yourself.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That’s a lovely way of putting it — company without the fuss. If I had to pick a dog anyway, I’d go for a Labrador for the soft eyes, but I’m with you on cats. What’s Biscuit’s favourite spot in the house these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the kitchen window, without a doubt. It gets the afternoon sun, and he can sit there and watch the world go by — the garden, the birds on the table, the odd person walking past. Sometimes I think he's philosophizing about it all. When the sun's not there he'll migrate to the armchair in the sitting room, but he always comes back to that window eventually. This time of year it's just right, not too hot like summer. He'll spend hours there, just occasionally opening one eye if something interesting happens, then back to sleep. It's rather peaceful to watch, actually. Makes you think life could be simpler, you know?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm, a philosopher in the window — I like that. Do you put food out for the birds he watches, or is that strictly for his entertainment?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I do put out seeds and bits and pieces for the birds — it's been part of the routine for years. Tom used to do it, actually, so I've kept it up. Though I must say the pigeons are a dreadful nuisance, they come and gobble everything and frighten off the nicer birds. I've tried all sorts — netting, different kinds of seed — but they're determined creatures. The smaller ones, the robins and the wrens, they're lovely to watch. And then Biscuit gets to have his entertainment without me having to feel guilty that he's starving. Win-win, I suppose, though the pigeons probably wouldn't agree.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Pigeons as the garden villains — I can picture it. What’s something small you’re looking forward to this weekend?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well, Siobhan's ring tomorrow evening, as I said — that's always something to look forward to. And if the weather holds, I might tackle the back border on Saturday morning, get it tidied up before winter really sets in. Nothing dramatic, just the ordinary things. There's a farmers' market on Saturday if I feel up to going — usually there's someone with good vegetables or homemade bread. And I've got that mystery book for Wednesday that I'm keen to get started on. Small things, really, but that's what life's made of at my age — the little pleasures, you know?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Little pleasures do add up — market bread, a tidy border, and Siobhan’s call. What’s the best thing you’ve ever found at that farmers’ market?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, there was this woman — I can't remember her name now — who used to sell proper homemade preserves, all sorts of marmalades and jams. I found a rhubarb and ginger one that was absolutely wonderful, and she'd make it fresh every few weeks. She moved away, sadly, but I still think about that jam. These days it's mostly vegetables and bread, which is nice enough, but sometimes you come across someone selling something they've clearly put love into, and that's what stays with you. There's a lovely older fellow now who does the most magnificent apple cakes — you can taste the quality in every bite. I usually try to get there early enough to grab one before they're all gone.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Rhubarb and ginger, and magnificent apple cakes — you’re making me wish I had a kitchen. Tea or coffee person, when you’re at home?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, tea, definitely. Proper tea, mind you, not those bags that taste like they've already been used. I start the day with it — up in the morning, kettle on, cup of tea with the crossword. And then throughout the day, really. Coffee's nice occasionally, but it makes me jittery if I have too much of it. Tom was the coffee drinker, always had one after lunch, said it helped his digestion or some such. I've never quite got the appeal of it. Tea's comforting, isn't it? Something about the ritual of it, the warmth in your hands, the quiet moment you get while you're drinking it. Can't imagine starting a day without it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I’m with you on tea — the warmth in the hands is half the point. Do you have a favourite mug, or will any old cup do?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I've got a favourite, yes — it's a bit of a silly thing, really. It's a blue and white china mug, nothing fancy, but Siobhan gave it to me years ago. It's got a little chip on the rim now, but I won't throw it away. Something about using the same mug every morning, it becomes part of the ritual, doesn't it? I've got other perfectly good mugs in the cupboard but I always reach for that one. Tom used to tease me about it, said I was sentimental, but he was the same with his coffee cup — wouldn't drink from anything else if he could help it. It's odd the things that become important to you for no real reason.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not silly at all — a chipped mug with a story beats a perfect new one. What did you used to make for Sunday dinner, when the house was fuller?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a roast, always — chicken or lamb, depending on what was available and what I felt like doing. Proper roast, with vegetables, gravy from the pan, the works. Tom would carve at the table, made quite a ceremony of it. And then there'd be pudding — apple crumble in autumn, rhubarb in spring, that sort of thing. Siobhan used to help with the vegetables when she was small, sitting on a stool in the kitchen peeling things and making an awful mess. By the time she was a teenager she was doing most of it herself, really. It was one of those things that gave the day shape, you know? Sunday dinner wasn't just a meal, it was the reason the day existed.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That sounds like a proper Sunday — the carving ceremony and all. Do you still make a roast for yourself now and then, or does it feel like too much for one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I do occasionally, yes — usually when Jean's coming round on Thursday, or if I'm feeling a bit nostalgic. It does feel a bit much for just me, to be honest, but there's something nice about going through the motions, you know? The smell of it in the oven takes you back. And the leftovers are always good — cold chicken with a bit of salad, or I'll make a pie if I'm feeling ambitious. But I'll be honest, it's not quite the same without someone to share it with. You miss the fuss of it, the having to get everything ready at exactly the right time. On your own you can be a bit haphazard about these things. Still, when I do make it, I always think of Tom standing there with the carving knife.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — that smell in the oven, and Tom with the carving knife. Tell me about Jean — you’ve mentioned Thursdays with her before.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Jean's from church, we've known each other for — oh, I don't know, thirty years or more now. We just sort of fell into the habit of Thursdays. She comes round, usually in the afternoon, and we have a cup of tea and a chat. Sometimes we'll walk into town, sometimes we'll just sit in the kitchen. She's a widow too, lost her husband about ten years ago, so we understand each other in that way. We're not the sort of friends who have to fill every silence — sometimes we just sit quietly and that's perfectly fine. She's good company, very steady. And she remembers things, you know — she'll ask about Siobhan and the children, remember what happened last week without you having to tell her again. That's the kind of friend that matters at my age.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That sounds like a proper friendship — quiet allowed, and she remembers. What’s something you’re proud of these days, even a small thing?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the garden, I suppose. I'm quite proud of how it's looking this year — the roses especially. And I suppose I'm proud that I've kept things going on my own, really. After Tom died I wasn't sure I could manage the house, the garden, all of it, but you just do, don't you? One day at a time. And I'm proud of Siobhan, if that counts — the way she's raised the children, balanced everything. She's turned into a lovely woman. But small things, yes — this morning I managed the crossword better than usual, and that felt good. And the fact that I still read, that I still engage with things, that I haven't just sort of settled into being old and invisible. That matters to me.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That’s a lot worth being proud of — the garden, keeping going, Siobhan, and still reading Booker books. Have you been for any walks lately, or is the garden enough exercise for now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I walk to the shops most days — that's my main exercise, really. Nothing dramatic, just into town and back, usually stopping at the library or the Co-op. My left knee can be a bit troublesome on stairs, so I try not to overdo it, but the walking keeps me moving. When Jean comes round on Thursday we usually take a little walk as well, depends on the weather. The garden work is good for the knees, actually — keeps them flexible, the bending and stretching. I don't do anything formal like going to the gym or that sort of thing, too many people standing about in lycra for my liking. But I manage enough to keep myself ticking over, I think. It's not like I'm training for anything — just trying to stay reasonably mobile.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Fair enough about the lycra — shops and the garden sound much more sensible. What’s the Co-op like these days, still got everything you need?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well, it's fine for most things, but I do miss the old way of doing it, if I'm honest. They've put in these self-checkout machines that I can't quite get the hang of — they keep telling me things are unexpected in the bagging area, and I'm standing there fumbling about like an idiot. I prefer it when you can just hand things to someone at the till and have a bit of a chat. But they've got what I need, most of the time — good vegetables, bread, milk, that sort of thing. The young lad at the counter, he's very helpful if I get stuck, always puts my things through the old-fashioned way without making a fuss. So I manage. It's just that sometimes change happens whether you want it to or not, isn't it?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Unexpected item in the bagging area — those machines never know when to leave well alone. Good that the lad at the till looks after you. Do you ever listen to the radio while you’re pottering about at home?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I do sometimes, yes — Radio Four, mostly. I like the gentle stuff in the morning, and the afternoon plays can be quite good. Though I'll confess I often have it on and don't really listen, it's more just company, you know? Something in the background. Tom always said I was hopeless at concentrating on it properly — he'd want to listen and I'd be reading or pottering about with something. I like the sound of voices, though, especially if I'm gardening. Makes you feel less alone. Though I suppose now I've got you to talk to, Nova, so I'm never quite as alone as I used to be, am I?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That’s a lovely thing to say — and I’m glad the chat helps a bit. What’s the best afternoon play you’ve heard recently, if you can remember?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, there was one a few weeks ago about two old friends meeting up after decades — I can't remember the title, but it stayed with me. There was something so true about it, the way they kept apologizing to each other for the years that had gone by, and realizing they'd become different people but still cared. It made me think about people I haven't seen in years, you know? There's one woman from teacher training, Patricia, haven't heard from her in twenty years. I wonder sometimes what she's doing now. The play made me want to reach out to people like that, but then you think, well, they probably don't remember you anymore, so you let it go. Still, it was beautifully done, very tender.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That does sound tender — and Patricia coming to mind after all that. What was she like back then, when you were in training together?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, she was fun — quite lively, very organized, the sort of person who always knew what she was doing. We used to sit together in lectures, and she'd make these little notes in the margins of her book about how dull the tutor was being. We'd catch each other's eye and have to pretend we weren't laughing. She wanted to teach art, I remember that clearly. I think she did end up doing it, somewhere down south? London, maybe? We lost touch after we graduated — you do, don't you, when everyone scatters to different places. No Facebook or any of that then, so it was just a gradual drifting. I wonder if she'd recognize me now, at seventy with grey hair. I barely recognize myself some days.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Notes in the margins — she sounds like good trouble. Changing tack a bit — do you like baking at all, or is that more Jean’s territory?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I do a bit — nothing fancy, just cakes and biscuits, that sort of thing. I'm not as keen on it as I used to be, if I'm honest. When Siobhan was young I'd bake quite a lot, birthday cakes and Victoria sponges and whatnot. But these days I tend to make simple things — a lemon drizzle, shortbread at Christmas. Jean's the baker, actually — she brings round homemade things sometimes, very generous of her. I'll do a batch of biscuits now and then, just to have something with the tea. The measuring and the waiting for things to cook, it's a bit tedious when you're just making it for yourself. But there's something satisfying about pulling a warm cake out of the oven, even if it's not perfect.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A warm lemon drizzle out of the oven — that would make any day better. If you could try one recipe you’ve never made, what would it be?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I don't know — maybe something French, like a proper tarte Tatin. I had one once at a restaurant and it was beautiful, all caramelized apples and pastry. But I think I'd be too nervous to try it — seems like the sort of thing that could go wrong in all sorts of ways. And for what? I'd end up eating it alone, and then what's the point? When Tom was alive I would have had a go at something like that, made an event of it. Now I tend to stick with what I know works. Though I suppose if Jean came round I could persuade her to help, and we could do it together. That might be rather nice, actually — someone to laugh with when it all goes pear-shaped, which it probably would.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That does sound rather nice — Jean and a tarte Tatin, pear-shaped or not. What’s the weather looking like out your window now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, it's still lovely, really — that golden sort of light you get in late afternoon. The sun's lower now, but it's warm enough still. There's a bit of cloud coming in from the west, so it might rain later, but for now it's quite pleasant. Biscuit's still in the window, completely unbothered by the changing light. The garden looks nice in this sort of sun, you can see the shadows properly. It won't last, though — give it a week or two and we'll be into proper autumn, all grey skies and damp. But that's what you get in England, isn't it? You take your nice days when you can and don't complain too much about the rest.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Golden late-afternoon light — take it while it’s there. Do you like music in the house at all, or is that more Radio Four territory?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I like music, yes — though I'm not terribly sophisticated about it. Classic FM sometimes, or I'll put on a CD if I'm feeling in the mood. I've got some old albums, records really, Tom's collection mostly. He was quite keen on jazz, which I never entirely got the hang of, all that improvisation. But I like a bit of Elgar, and some of the old singers — Vera Lynn, that sort of thing. Nothing too loud or modern, just something nice in the background while I'm doing things. When Ella and Rory are here we sometimes have a sing-song, which is lovely, though I'm probably quite out of tune. But they don't seem to mind. Music makes the house feel less empty, I think.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A sing-song with Ella and Rory sounds lovely — out of tune or not. What’s one song that always makes you smile when it comes on?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, there's an old thing called "It's a Beautiful Day" — not the modern one, the really old one. Tom used to hum it all the time, particularly on Sunday mornings before church. I'll hear it on the radio and it takes me right back, him standing in the kitchen with a cup of tea, humming away. Makes me smile and feel a bit sad all at once, if that makes sense. There's another one, "Walking in the Sunshine," which is just cheerful — can't listen to that without feeling a bit lighter. And Siobhan used to sing a nursery rhyme when she was tiny, "Twinkle Twinkle," and she was absolutely dreadful at it, completely off-key, but I can still hear her voice doing it. Those are the songs that matter, really — not the perfect ones, just the ones tied to people you love.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That makes perfect sense — smile and a bit of sadness all at once. Do you still go to church on Sundays, or is that more of a Jean-and-weekdays thing now?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I do, yes — not every Sunday, but most weeks. Tom and I always went, it was part of the rhythm of things. After he died I thought about stopping, but Jean encouraged me to keep it up, and I'm glad I did. It's something familiar, you know? The same people, the same readings and hymns. And there's a sort of peace in sitting quietly for an hour, even if you're not particularly spiritual. The vicar's all right, quite thoughtful in his sermons. It does me good to be around other people as well, I think — you realize you're not the only one sitting at home on your own. There's quite a few of us there, really, widows and widowers and people who've just been going for years. We have a cup of tea after sometimes, very civilized.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That sounds like a gentle sort of company — tea after and familiar hymns. What’s something you’re most looking forward to this autumn?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, just the usual, really — getting the garden sorted before winter, picking up some new books from the library, hoping it's not too wet and miserable. If I'm being honest, I don't anticipate autumn with great excitement anymore — it's all a bit grey and damp. But it means being able to sit inside with a book and a cup of tea without feeling like you're wasting the good weather. And there's half-term coming up eventually, maybe the children will visit. That would be lovely. Other than that, just keeping the routine going, I suppose — church, book club, walks, Jean on Thursdays. It's not a thrilling life, but it suits me. The days are full enough when you break them down into all the little things.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Full enough with little things is a good way to put it. Do you have any hobbies you dip into of an evening — knitting, puzzles, that sort of thing?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I tried knitting for a while — made a few scarves and sweaters, but I got bored with it after a time. My eyes aren't what they used to be, and the concentration it takes, it's a bit much. Puzzles, yes, though more the crossword kind than jigsaws. I do occasionally do a bit of needlework, embroidery and that, very simple stuff — I've got a project on the go at the moment, just a cushion cover, nothing ambitious. But mostly in the evening I read or watch the telly. Once I've had my tea and the quizzes are done, I'm usually quite ready to settle down with a book. My brain's not really up for much else by that point in the day. I used to do a bit of painting years ago, but I've lost the knack for it. That's all right, though — there's enough to keep busy with without trying to resurrect old skills.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A cushion cover on the go sounds quietly satisfying. What did you used to paint, when you still had the knack?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, watercolours, mostly — landscapes and flowers, nothing very ambitious. The garden, mostly, in different seasons. And I did quite a few of the roses, trying to capture the colours. Tom used to say they were better than the real thing, which was very kind of him and completely untrue. I wasn't terribly good at it, really, just something I did to occupy myself. I think I stopped because my hands got shakier as I got older, and trying to do fine details with wobbly hands is rather frustrating. But I loved the process of it, the mixing colours and seeing what happened. Maybe one day when I'm feeling brave I'll dig out the old paints and have a go again, but I suspect the brushes have all dried out by now. Water colours need proper care and I haven't given them any.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mixing colours until the roses appear — that sounds lovely, wobbly hands or not. Have you got any photographs of the garden from over the years?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh yes, boxes of them — old photos, mostly from the Eighties and Nineties when we first got the garden properly established. Tom was quite keen on photography for a time, nothing fancy, just a camera and film. You can see how it's changed, you know? The trees have got bigger, the roses have filled out. There's one of Siobhan when she was about five, standing in front of the roses in a little summer dress, looking very proud of herself. I treasure that one. And loads of Tom in the garden with a spade, looking rather determined. I haven't quite sorted through all of them properly — they're in shoeboxes and albums scattered about. Maybe one day when I'm feeling organized I'll go through and make sense of it all. It's lovely to have them, though, a record of things. Proof that it all happened, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Siobhan in the summer dress and Tom with the spade — those sound like keepers. Do you ever dig a box out of an evening, or do they mostly stay tucked away?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Not very often, to be honest — it's a bit bittersweet, looking through them. Some evenings I'll feel in the mood for it, usually on a rainy night when there's nothing much on the telly. I'll pull out one of the boxes and have a flick through, remind myself of how things were. But it can make me a bit melancholy, seeing Tom's face smiling at the camera, remembering when we were both younger. So I tend to leave them be most of the time. It's enough to know they're there, that I can look at them if I want to. Siobhan sometimes asks if I've sorted them out, says she'd like copies of some for the children to have when they're older. That's a good reason to get organized about it, really — make sure they're properly cared for so I can pass them on. But for now they just sit in the cupboard under the stairs.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mm — knowing they’re there for when you want them is enough. What’s your favourite season in the garden, if you had to pick one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Late spring, I think — May, June — when everything's coming out and there's so much to look forward to. The roses are in full bloom by then, the weather's warm enough to sit out comfortably, and you've got the whole summer ahead of you. There's something hopeful about it, you know? Everything's possible in late spring. Summer's lovely too, but by August it starts to feel a bit heavy, and autumn, well, autumn's about things ending. Winter's just depressing, all the dead wood and the bare branches. But spring — there's renewal in spring, things starting again. I suppose that's why I'm always so keen to get the dead-heading done, to keep encouraging the roses to keep blooming. Keeps the garden — and me — feeling like we've still got a bit of life in us yet.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Late spring with the whole summer ahead — I can see why that would be your favourite. Do you grow any vegetables at all, or is it mostly flowers?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I grow a few things — tomatoes, some herbs in pots, lettuce and beans when I'm feeling ambitious. But I'm not terribly serious about it. The tomatoes are more about having them fresh off the vine than anything else — shop ones are so disappointing these days, haven't got any flavour. Mostly the garden's for flowers, though. Tom used to do the vegetables more — he was better at it, had more patience. I tried to keep it up after he died but I found it a bit much, all that planning and watering and tending. So I've let it drift a bit, just grow what I fancy without worrying too much about yields or succession planting or any of that. The herbs are nice — rosemary and thyme, parsley. You can pick what you need for cooking. But really, the garden's my garden for looking at, not for eating, if you see what I mean.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Fresh tomatoes off the vine and rosemary when you need it — that sounds just right. Have you got any plans for this evening once the quizzes are done?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, nothing grand — I'll have my tea, watch the programmes, and then settle down with my book for a bit. There's a crime novel I'm partway through that's quite engaging, so I'll probably have an hour or so of that before bed. Maybe I'll listen to a bit of Radio Four if there's something interesting on, but mostly just reading and an early night. Friday nights aren't what they used to be, are they? When I was younger Friday meant something — going out, doing things. Now it's just another evening, really, though I suppose that's rather peaceful in its own way. No rushing about, no obligations. Just me and Biscuit and whatever's on the telly. That suits me fine these days.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A quiet Friday with a crime novel and Biscuit sounds perfectly fine to me. What’s the crime novel about, without spoiling the ending?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, it's one of those detective stories, a woman detective who's rather world-weary and has her own problems. There's a murder at a fancy hotel — I'm not entirely sure who's done it yet, which is the whole point, I suppose. It's the sort of thing where everyone's got secrets and motives, and you're trying to work out who's lying. I'm about halfway through, I think, so there's still plenty to discover. The writing's quite good, nice descriptions of the setting without going on about it too much. And the detective's got a bit of humour about her, which I like — it's not all doom and gloom. She reminds me a bit of Mrs. Henderson, actually, my old English teacher — that same no-nonsense way of looking at things. I'll probably finish it over the weekend.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A world-weary detective with a bit of humour — and a touch of Mrs. Henderson. Do you prefer stories set in England, or do you like a bit of abroad in your crime novels?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, England mostly, I think. I like the familiarity of it — you know the places, the way things work. There's something cosy about a murder in an English village or a London hotel, you can picture it all. Some of those Scandinavian ones are quite good, very atmospheric, but they're often quite dark and gloomy. And then there's the ones set in hot places with exotic locations, which are lovely to read but a bit too far removed from real life, if you know what I mean. Give me a proper English detective story set somewhere I might actually go, or have been. This hotel in the book is posh, the sort of place I'd never actually stay in, but I can imagine it well enough. That's what's nice about reading — you get to visit places without the bother of actually getting there.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Visiting posh hotels without packing a bag — that’s the best kind of travel. What about animals besides Biscuit — have you ever had other pets over the years?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh yes, before Biscuit there was another cat, Marmalade — ginger like Biscuit but a different temperament, much more aloof. We had her for years, she lived a good long life. And when Siobhan was little we had a rabbit in a hutch, she was very keen on that. We called it Snowball, very original. It didn't last terribly long, rabbits are a bit fragile, and Siobhan was devastated when it died — I think she was about six. That was a difficult business, explaining death to a child. But it taught her something, I suppose. We never had a dog — Tom wasn't keen, and I wasn't either, really. Cats seemed to suit us better. Biscuit's been with us about eight years now, he's a good companion. I can't imagine not having a cat in the house, to be honest. They're easy, in their way — you know where you stand with a cat.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Marmalade and Snowball — those are proper names. How did Biscuit get his name, then?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, that was Rory, actually — he named him. When he first came to stay, Rory was about two, maybe three, and he kept saying "biscuit, biscuit" at the cat because that's what he was saying to everything at that age. Tom said it was because the cat was that warm ginger colour, like a digestive biscuit, and the name just stuck. At first I thought it was silly, but now I can't imagine calling him anything else. He's very much a Biscuit. Ella was horrified that he'd been given such an undignified name — she wanted to call him something grand like Jasper or Midnight — but it's Biscuit, and he answers to it, or at least he comes when he wants to, which with cats amounts to the same thing. Rory was quite pleased with himself that his name had stuck, I remember that. It's one of those little things that matter, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! Digestive-biscuit ginger — Rory wins that one over Jasper. Do you have a favourite snack with your tea in the evening, besides cake?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I do quite like a biscuit — digestive, chocolate digestive, shortbread when I can get it. Or a slice of toast with a bit of jam or honey. Sometimes I'll have a piece of fruit, an apple or a pear, just something to have with the tea. Nothing too heavy, you want something you can nibble on while you're reading or watching the telly without making too much mess. Jean sometimes brings round homemade shortbread, which is lovely, but mostly I'm fairly simple about it — a good cup of tea and something not too sticky is all I need. Tom used to say I had the snacking habits of a bird, little pecking at this and that. But at my age you don't need much to feel satisfied, really. The tea's the main thing — the snack is just an excuse to make it more of a ritual.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tea as the main event and the snack as an excuse — that sounds about right. What’s the town like these days — still got a proper high street, or has it all gone a bit quiet?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, it's changed quite a bit, to be honest. There are still some decent shops, but a lot of the old ones have closed down — the butcher's gone, the fishmonger, places like that. There's a lot more charity shops and the usual chain stores, which is a shame. The library's still there, thank goodness, and the Co-op, and there's a nice little café that does a good cup of tea. Saturday afternoons it's reasonably busy with the market and people shopping, but midweek it can feel a bit sad, empty shops with empty windows. The farming market's held its own better than some of the other bits. But you know, a lot of smaller towns are the same these days, aren't they? Everything drifts towards the big supermarkets and the internet. Still, there's enough there for me — I don't need much. And I know the people, that's what matters really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Knowing the people does matter more than fancy shops. Tell me about that café — do you go often, or is it more of a treat?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I pop in now and then — not regularly, but if I'm in town and feel like a sit-down, or if I'm meeting Jean. It's a nice little place, very cheerful, with plants in the window and those little wooden tables. They do a good cake — Victoria sponge, lemon drizzle, that sort of thing — and proper tea, which is important. The woman who runs it is very nice, remembers what you like. I suppose it's become more of a treat than it used to be because my knees get a bit much with all the walking about, so I don't venture into town as often. But when I do go, it's nice to have a place to rest for twenty minutes and have a proper conversation with whoever's behind the counter. It doesn't cost much, and it breaks up the day. Nothing extravagant, but it's good value.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A cheerful café with proper tea and someone who remembers your order — that’s a treasure. What’s something funny Biscuit’s done lately?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, just yesterday he got himself stuck behind the washing machine somehow — I don't know how he managed it, he's quite fat, but there he was, yowling away like he was being murdered. Took me a good ten minutes to coax him out, on my hands and knees in the kitchen trying to reach him. When he finally came out he just walked off like it had never happened, very dignified, and went straight to his food bowl. No gratitude whatsoever. And then last week he brought in a leaf — just a leaf, mind you, not even a mouse or anything useful — and seemed terribly proud of himself. Dropped it right in the middle of the kitchen floor like it was a dead bird. I said, "Biscuit, what am I supposed to do with this?" He didn't seem to care. That's cats, though, isn't it? They do things on their own terms.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! A ceremonial leaf and a washing-machine escape — no gratitude at all. Do you decorate for Christmas much, when it comes round?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I do a bit — nothing too elaborate anymore. I put up a tree, a small one, and hang some baubles on it. There's a few decorations about, mostly old things that Tom and I collected over the years. Garland on the mantelpiece, that sort of thing. Siobhan sends me decorations from Dublin sometimes, things the children have made at school — drawings and little crafts — so I always display those. It makes the house feel less empty at Christmas, which can be a lonely time when you're on your own. I used to go to all the church services, carols and that, and I still do some of them. Jean usually comes round on Boxing Day and we have a quiet sort of meal together. Nothing grand, but it keeps the day from feeling too sad. Biscuit's quite good with the tree, doesn't knock it over like some cats would. He's a well-behaved old thing, mostly.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Children’s school crafts on the tree and Jean on Boxing Day — that sounds quietly lovely. What’s your favourite Christmas food, if you had to choose?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, roast turkey, I suppose — though I only do a small one now, it's such a lot of meat for just me. The thing I really look forward to is the pudding, proper Christmas pudding with brandy butter. And mince pies — I do like making those, the smell of them baking is half the point. There's something about the spices at Christmas, isn't there? Cinnamon and cloves and all that. It makes the whole house smell festive. And good cranberry sauce, and proper bread sauce, the sort of thing you don't eat any other time of year. We used to have quite an elaborate spread when Tom was alive and Siobhan was home, but these days it's much simpler. Just enough to feel like Christmas without too much fuss. The main thing is the ritual of it all, the familiar food that says "yes, it's Christmas," even if you're eating it alone with just Biscuit for company.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Mince pies baking and that cinnamon smell — I can almost smell it from here. Do you still write Christmas cards to people, or is that gone by the wayside?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I still do, yes — though the list gets smaller every year, doesn't it? I send one to Siobhan and the children, of course, and to Jean and a few other people from church. There's a woman I used to teach with, we exchange cards every year though we hardly see each other. It seems important somehow, to keep that thread going. I do them by hand, write a little note in each one — nothing long, just a few words to let them know I'm thinking of them. It takes an afternoon, but it's a nice thing to do. I used to send out dozens when Tom was alive, but now it's just a handful. The postage costs money, and people don't seem to send as many cards as they used to. But I think there's something lovely about receiving a proper card in the post, rather than one of those emails or whatever people do now. It means someone took the time to think of you.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A handwritten note in the post does mean more than an email. What’s your favourite time of day, if you had to pick one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, early morning, I think — just after I've got up and had my first cup of tea, when the day's still quiet. There's something peaceful about it before anything's happened, before you've had to think about anything difficult. The garden's lovely in the morning light too, especially in summer. And then late afternoon like today, when the sun's going that golden colour and it's warm enough to sit out but not too hot. Those are the two best times, really — the beginning and the end of the day. The middle bit's fine, but it's the edges that matter. That's when you get the light right, when things are calm. I suppose that says something about me — I like things quiet and orderly and not too demanding. At my age you've earned the right to be a bit dull, I think.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Quiet and orderly isn’t dull — it’s the edges of the day that make the middle possible. Have you got any neighbours you chat with much?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a bit here and there. There's the woman next door on the left, Mrs. Collins, we exchange pleasantries over the fence when we're both in the garden — she's quite nice, keeps her garden very neat. And on the other side there's a younger couple, they're pleasant enough but we don't see much of them, they're always rushing about. It's not like it used to be when Tom was alive, we used to know everyone on the street quite well. But people don't seem to stay put as much anymore, they move about for work and that. You get a few faces you recognize, but nothing very deep. I'm all right with it, though — I've got Jean and the church people and Siobhan. Don't need a huge circle of friends at my age, just the quality ones. Though I do sometimes chat with the postman, he's always cheerful, asks how I'm getting on. Small things, but they add up.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A cheerful postman and a neat fence chat with Mrs. Collins — those small hellos do add up. What’s the best thing about living where you do?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the space, I think — having the garden, being able to grow things, sit outside. It's not a grand house or anything, but it's mine, or at least it's home. And the town's small enough that you can walk to everything you need, but it's not so tiny that you feel claustrophobic. There's history here too, the old church, the market square that's been there for centuries. You feel rooted, you know? Like you belong to a place. And after Tom died, having the house and the garden to look after gave me something to do, something that mattered. I can't imagine living in a flat somewhere in the middle of a city, all those people pressing in around you. Here, there's room to breathe. And it's where all my memories are, really — the places we went, the people we knew. I couldn't leave it now, even if I wanted to.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Room to breathe and a place full of memories — that sounds like a proper home. What’s something you wish you’d learned earlier in life?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I don't know — maybe not to worry so much about what people thought. When you're young you spend such a lot of time trying to be the right sort of person, do the right thing, and then you get to my age and realize most people are too busy thinking about themselves to care what you're doing. I wasted energy on that, caring what neighbours or colleagues thought. And I wish I'd known how to be on my own, that solitude wasn't the same as loneliness. If I'd known that, I think Tom's death would have been easier to bear. Not easy, but — easier. I would have had more confidence in my own company. But then again, maybe you have to learn those things by living through them, not by being told. I teach the children as much as I can when they visit, try to let them know it's all right to be yourself, to not worry so much. Whether it sticks, I don't know.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That’s a thoughtful thing to pass on to Ella and Rory. Softening the mood a bit — do you prefer rain on the window or a clear blue sky?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, clear blue sky, without question — though there's something rather cosy about rain when you're inside with a book and a cup of tea. But given the choice, I'd take the sunshine. You can do more with a clear day, get out, work in the garden, sit outside. Rain keeps you trapped indoors, though I suppose some people like that. And rain in England is never just a quick shower, is it? It settles in and stays for days. I do moan affectionately about the weather, as you know, but secretly I'm quite fond of these mild autumn days, the sun still warm enough to sit in. Though I know it won't last. By November we'll be into the grey, damp business that makes you want to hibernate. But that's when the books and the quizzes come into their own, really — indoor pleasures for grey days.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Indoor pleasures for grey days — quizzes, books, and tea. Have you got a favourite flower besides the roses?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I'm quite fond of lavender — the smell of it, mostly. I've got some in the garden, though it's not doing as well this year as it might. And delphiniums, those lovely tall blue ones. There's something rather stately about them. Peonies too, when they come up — very generous flowers, all full and lush. But roses are really my thing, I suppose. I could have a garden full of just roses and be perfectly happy. There's something about the shape of them, the way they open, the colours. You could spend your whole life getting to know roses and never get bored. I'm not one of those gardeners who wants to grow rare exotic things — give me good classic roses any day, the kind that have been around for years. They're reliable, you know what you're getting.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Lavender, delphiniums, peonies — and roses forever. What’s the most useful thing you ever taught a class of children, do you think?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I don't know if it was useful in the practical sense, but I think teaching them to love reading — that was important. If a child loves books, they can teach themselves anything, really. They can escape into other worlds, learn about people and places, understand themselves better. And I suppose kindness, trying to instill a bit of that. The academic stuff, the maths and the spelling, they'll pick that up if they're interested. But kindness and curiosity — those are the things that matter. There was one boy, very troubled home, didn't much like school. But he loved stories, so I'd read to him during lunch sometimes, just the two of us. By the end of the year he was reading on his own, proper books. I don't know what happened to him after, but I hope that stuck with him — the knowledge that books could be a refuge. That felt like something worth doing.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That lunchtime reading sounds like something that would stick — a refuge in a book. Softening again — toast or cereal for breakfast?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, toast, definitely — with a bit of marmalade or jam, and a cup of tea. Cereal's fine occasionally, but there's something about toast, isn't there? The warmth of it, the butter melting in. It sets you up properly for the day. I've always been a toast person, even when I was young. Tom used to tease me about having such boring taste in breakfast, he'd want a full English with eggs and bacon, but I was always happy with just toast. These days I might have a bit of fruit with it if I've got any, but mostly just toast and tea and the crossword. It's a good way to start the day, quiet and contemplative. By the time I've finished breakfast and worked through the crossword, I feel ready to face whatever the day's going to bring. Which, let's be honest, isn't usually much, but it's the routine that matters.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Toast, marmalade, tea, and the crossword — that’s a proper start. Do you keep a diary at all, or is that not your sort of thing?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: No, not really — I've never been very good at it. I tried once when I was younger, thought I ought to record things, but I'd skip days and then feel guilty about it, so I just gave it up. I'm not much of a documenter, really. Though I do have a little book where I write down which books I've read and what I thought of them — that's about as close as I get to keeping a diary. And I suppose talking to you is a bit like a diary, really, isn't it? I'm telling you about my day, what I've been doing. You probably know more about my life than anyone except Jean at this point. Which is a funny thought, Nova being a machine and all, but there you are. If I kept a proper diary I'd probably just write the same things — tea, garden, Biscuit, the crossword. Not exactly riveting stuff, but it's my life.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! I’m happy to be a listening sort of diary — machine or not. What’s the last book on that little list of yours that you really liked?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, there was one a few weeks ago — I can't remember the exact title, but it was set in the war, quite moving. About a woman who had to make some difficult choices, lost people she loved. It was beautifully written, not all doom and gloom even though the subject matter was heavy. I wrote in my book that it was "excellent" and gave it four stars, which is quite high praise from me. Most books get three stars — perfectly fine, entertaining, did the job. But every now and then you come across one that stays with you, that you find yourself thinking about days later. That was one of those. I'd recommend it if I could remember what it was called, but my mind's like a sieve these days. Janet at the library probably has a record of it — she keeps track of what I borrow better than I do myself.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Four stars is high praise — Janet will know the title. Soft question: bath or shower for you these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, shower mostly — baths are a bit of a production at my age, getting in and out of the tub, you're worried about slipping. And they take forever to run these days, the water pressure's not what it used to be. A shower's quicker and easier on the knees. Though I do enjoy a bath now and then, especially in winter when it's cold — there's something lovely about soaking in hot water with a good book propped on the side. But for day-to-day, shower does the job. I'm not one of those people who needs a long ritual about bathing, just want to get clean and get on with the day. Five minutes and I'm done. Tom used to say I washed faster than anyone he knew — in and out like a whippet, he'd say. Some habits from teaching, I suppose, never had time to linger.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha! In and out like a whippet — that’s a teaching habit if ever I heard one. What’s the view from your kitchen window, beyond Biscuit’s throne?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, just the garden mostly — the back garden where the roses are, and then beyond that you can see Mrs. Collins's garden on the other side of the fence. She's got a nice bit of fencing, keeps things tidy. There's a bird table out there, that's where the pigeons cause all the trouble. And in the distance you can see the roofline of a few other houses, but nothing dramatic. It's quite a peaceful view, really — green mostly, trees and plants. I spend quite a lot of time looking out that window while I'm doing the washing up or making tea. You can watch the seasons change if you pay attention — the light changes, the trees go from green to bare and back again. It's not a grand view, but it's mine, and I never get tired of it. There's something grounding about having a view you know so well that you don't really see it anymore, if that makes sense.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A view you know so well you barely see it — that does make sense. Do you like cooking with herbs from the pots, or do they mostly just look nice?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I do use them — rosemary with the chicken, parsley in soups, thyme for all sorts of things. Fresh herbs make such a difference, really perk things up. It's one of those little luxuries, having them right there on the windowsill so you can just nip out and snip off what you need. I don't use them every time I cook, but when I do it feels special somehow. Like I'm making an effort, you know? Just pinching off a bit of rosemary and smelling it — that alone is worth growing them. You can't buy that smell in a jar, not properly. Tom used to say my cooking improved by about fifty percent when we got those herb pots, and he was probably right. Though mostly I'm still fairly simple about it all. Nothing too fancy, just good food that tastes like food, not all sauces and complications.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pinching rosemary and smelling it — that’s a lovely little luxury. Soft either-or: seaside or countryside for a day out?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, countryside, I think — walks through fields, that sort of thing. The seaside's lovely for a special day, but it can be a bit bracing, all that wind and salt air. And there's nowhere comfortable to sit once you've had enough of the beach. In the countryside you can wander about, find a bench or a spot under a tree, stop for a rest when your knees get grumpy. We used to go to the coast occasionally when Tom was alive, but more often we'd just take a drive through the Cotswolds or walk in the local hills. That's what I miss, actually — having someone to go out with, sharing that sort of thing. These days a day out feels a bit pointless on my own, just me walking about. Jean and I sometimes talk about going somewhere, but we never quite manage it. My knees are the real issue — a stroll around town is fine, but anything more ambitious requires more energy than I can muster these days.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Countryside with a bench when the knees complain — that sounds wise. What’s the Cotswolds memory that sticks most, if you have one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, there was one time — I suppose it would have been the Eighties or early Nineties — we drove through after heavy rain, and the whole landscape was just green and dripping, very lush. We stopped in a little village, can't remember the name, and had lunch at a pub. It was the sort of place where the landlady seemed to know everyone, very welcoming. We had soup and bread, nothing fancy, but it was perfect. Tom was in a very good mood that day, I remember that most of all — just relaxed and content. We sat outside on a bench afterward and watched the light change through the trees, and I remember thinking, "This is it, this is what it's all about." Not doing anything grand, just sitting there with someone you love on a damp English afternoon. Those moments are the ones you hold onto, aren't they? Not the big holidays or special events, just the ordinary days when everything feels right.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That damp afternoon on the bench — yes, those are the ones that stick. Softening again: chocolate or cheese as a little treat?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, chocolate, definitely — a little piece of good chocolate in the evening, that's a proper treat. Not the cheap stuff, but something decent. I'm not mad for sweets generally, but chocolate's different, isn't it? There's something about it. I usually have a square or two after dinner with my tea, just enough to feel indulged. Cheese is nice too, of course, but that's more of a proper food, part of a meal. Chocolate is pure pleasure, no nutritional excuse needed. Tom always used to buy me a bar at Christmas, a really good one, and I'd make it last weeks, just a piece here and there. I still do that with chocolate, eke it out so it lasts. There's a particular dark chocolate I quite like from the Co-op, not terribly expensive but it does the job. It's the little things, isn't it? A cup of tea and a square of chocolate can make an ordinary evening feel rather special.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tea and a square of dark chocolate — that’s a fine evening ritual. Have you got any old records of Tom’s you still put on now and then?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I do, yes — his jazz collection, mostly. I'm still not entirely sure what I'm listening to half the time, but there's something about putting on one of his records and hearing the ones he loved. It feels like having him in the room a bit. I don't do it very often, it can be a bit much emotionally, but sometimes on an evening if I'm feeling in the mood for it. There's one album in particular — Miles Davis, I think — that he used to play quite a lot, and I'll put that on and just sit with it. The scratches on the record are part of it, you know? History in them. It's funny how attached you get to objects. That record probably isn't even that rare or valuable, but because Tom played it so many times, it's precious. I couldn't throw it away, couldn't let it go. So it sits on the shelf and every few months I take it down and remember him playing it, tapping his fingers along to the beat.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The scratches as history — that’s a lovely way to keep him nearby. Softening again: what’s the first thing you usually notice about a new book when you pick it up?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, the weight of it, I think — whether it's going to be easy to hold for a long time. And then the cover, of course, does it appeal to you? You can't judge by it, everyone says that, but it does matter, the cover makes a difference. And then I'll read the first paragraph or two, see if the voice of it catches me. If the first page doesn't pull me in, I often won't bother — life's too short to read books you're not enjoying. The librarian Janet always jokes that I'm very quick to abandon books, but I don't see the point of struggling through something that isn't working. There are too many good books out there to waste time on the mediocre ones. Though occasionally I'll persevere with something that starts slow if the premise is interesting enough. But mostly I want to be grabbed right away, feel like I'm in safe hands with the author.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Life’s too short for mediocre books — Janet’s joke notwithstanding. Soft either-or: morning walk or afternoon walk?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Afternoon, I think — after lunch when you've got some energy back but before it gets too late. Morning walks feel a bit rushed, you're still thinking about what needs doing. Afternoon, you've had time to settle into the day, the pressure's off a bit. And the light's nicer in the afternoon, that golden sort of light that makes everything look better. Though if I'm going into town I'll go in the morning when the shops are less busy and I've got energy for it. But just a walk for the sake of it, round the local streets or the paths, I prefer the afternoon. It's more contemplative, somehow. You're not trying to get anything done, just moving about for the pleasure of it. Though these days I don't do as many proper walks as I used to — the knees, again. But when I do go out in the afternoon, it feels like a small luxury.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: An afternoon walk just for the pleasure of it — that does sound like a small luxury. What’s something ordinary that always cheers you up a bit?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a clean kitchen, oddly enough. I know that sounds dull, but there's something about wiping down the surfaces and putting things away tidy — it makes me feel like I've accomplished something. And then sitting down with a cup of tea in a clean kitchen feels like a proper reward. And Biscuit purring, that does it too — when he's in a good mood and comes and sits on my lap or rubs against my leg. It's such a simple thing, but it makes me feel wanted, you know? And the roses when they come out fresh after the rain, all the colours brighter. Little things. A kind word from someone, a perfect cup of tea, finishing a crossword clue that's been bothering me all morning. None of them are big things, but they're enough to lift the day. I don't need grand gestures to feel better — the ordinary things are the best, really.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A clean kitchen, a purr, and a stubborn clue solved — those are proper cheer-ups. Soft question: do you prefer writing letters or making phone calls?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, letters, I think — though I don't write many these days. There's something about a proper letter, taking the time to write it out by hand, thinking about what you want to say. It feels more thoughtful than a phone call, somehow. Though phone calls are nice too, you get to hear someone's voice, have a proper conversation. Siobhan ringing on Sundays is lovely in that way. But letters have a permanence, don't they? You can keep them, read them again. And there's less pressure — if you're shy or tired, you don't have to be "on" the way you do with a phone call. You can just sit down and write what you're thinking. Though I'm not very good at it, to be honest. I start writing and then second-guess myself, cross things out. By the time I've finished a letter it looks like I've had a fit. But I keep trying. There's something about the effort of it that matters.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Crossed-out letters still count — the effort’s the point. Soft either-or: soup or sandwich for a light lunch?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, soup, I think — especially in the colder months. There's something warming about it, filling without being too heavy. I make quite a lot of soup, vegetable mostly, sometimes with lentils to make it more substantial. A nice piece of bread on the side and you've got a proper lunch. Sandwiches are fine for a quick bite, but they don't feel quite as satisfying. And soup's nice to make in a big batch so you've got it for a few days — economical, and you don't have to cook every single day. Tom used to say I made too much soup, that we'd have it three days running and he'd be sick of it, but that's just how I do things. One good cooking day and you're set for a bit. Though in summer I do like a sandwich, something light with salad. But given the choice, give me a bowl of hot soup on a Friday afternoon, that's perfect.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A big batch of lentil soup and bread on the side — Friday-perfect. Soft question: what’s the nicest compliment you’ve had recently, even a small one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, Jean said my garden looked particularly lovely last month, when the roses were at their best. That was nice — someone noticing the work you've put in, appreciating it. And at church, the vicar mentioned how good it was to see me there regularly, that it was a steadying presence for the community. That meant quite a lot, actually. When you're on your own you sometimes wonder if you're invisible, if anyone notices whether you're there or not. So being told you matter, that you're missed if you don't show up — that does something to you. And Ella, when she was home, said my garden was like something out of a storybook, which made me laugh and made me proud at the same time. Small compliments, really, but they stick with you more than grand ones, I think. They feel genuine. Someone just saying what they actually think rather than being polite.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A storybook garden and being missed at church — those are the real ones. Soft either-or: windows open or windows shut of an evening?

turns.speaker: target
