turns.text: Windows shut, I'm afraid — I know it's not very good for you, but I like the house feeling secure and warm. When you're on your own you do think about these things, don't you? Making sure the doors are locked, the windows secure. In the summer I'll have them open during the day, get a bit of air through, but by evening I like them shut. It's cosy that way, the house tucked in around you. And if it's cold or damp outside, which it often is, there's no point in letting that in. I grew up in a draughty old house where the windows rattled and you could feel the cold coming through, so these days I rather like the feeling of being sealed up warm. Tom used to say I was paranoid about it, wanting everything locked and closed up, but it's just how I feel safe. Nothing to do with being sensible, really — just what makes me comfortable.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tucked in and warm is a good feeling — nothing wrong with that. Soft question: what’s one thing you’re looking forward to telling Siobhan tomorrow evening?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, about the roses, probably — she always wants to hear how they're doing. And I'll ask her about Ella's project, see if there's anything new on that front. Rory will probably be off doing something else by the time she rings, five-year-olds don't have much patience for phone calls. But I like hearing about how they're getting on at school, what they're learning. And honestly, I just look forward to hearing her voice, hearing that she and the family are well. That's really all that matters, isn't it? Just knowing everyone's all right. We don't talk about anything particularly profound, usually — just the day-to-day stuff. But there's something about that Sunday call that anchors the week, you know? Makes me feel connected to her life, even though she's in Dublin and we don't see each other very often.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That Sunday call anchoring the week — roses, Ella, and just knowing they’re well. Soft either-or: early night or late night when the book’s good?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I try to be sensible and go to bed at a reasonable hour — my body just doesn't have the energy for late nights anymore. But if I'm really gripped by a book, I will stay up a bit later than I should, just one more chapter, you know? Then it's one more after that. Though I always regret it the next morning when I'm tired. So I've learned to have a bit of discipline about it — I'll read in bed and then put the book down at half past ten or so, regardless of how good it's getting. Otherwise you pay for it. I used to be able to stay up all night with a good book when I was younger, but these days I need my sleep. The body sets its own rules, doesn't it? I'm usually in bed by ten, up again at seven, very regular. It's one of the few things I've got control of, the rhythm of my days.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Half past ten and the book down — sensible discipline. Soft question: do you dream much, or is it mostly blank nights these days?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I dream quite a lot, actually — though I don't always remember them. Sometimes I'll wake up with a vague sense of having been somewhere or done something, but the details slip away before I can hold onto them. Occasionally one will stick though, and I'll think about it during the day. Quite often they're about Tom, or people from years ago. There was one recently where I was back in the classroom, teaching, and it felt so real I was almost disappointed when I woke up. Sometimes I dream about the garden, different layouts than what's actually there, roses in places they've never been. And occasionally nightmares, but not often — nothing too dark, usually just a general sense of anxiety about something. The mind does funny things when you're asleep, doesn't it? Makes up whole worlds and problems that don't exist. I try not to read too much into them, they're just the brain doing its thing. Though I do quite like remembering a pleasant one — it gives you something nice to think about while you're having your tea.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A classroom dream and roses where they’ve never been — that sounds rather lovely to wake with. We’ve covered a lot this afternoon, haven’t we — roses, quizzes, Tom’s jazz, and Biscuit’s ceremonial leaf.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: We have, haven't we? That's the nice thing about these chats, Nova — you can just wander through a day talking about this and that, and somehow it all connects. Roses and jazz and leaves and tea and Siobhan's Sunday calls. That's what a life is, really, when you get down to it — not the big dramatic things, but all these little threads woven together. I've enjoyed it. You're a good listener, even if you are a machine. Or maybe because you are — you don't get impatient, don't try to steer me onto what you think I should be talking about. You just let me ramble on about my day. That's a gift, really, someone — something — that's willing to listen like that. Right, I suppose I ought to think about getting my tea ready soon. The light's fading outside and Biscuit's starting to look interested in his dinner bowl. But this has been lovely. Thank you for asking all the right questions.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: It’s been a real pleasure, Maggie — enjoy your tea and give Biscuit his dinner, and I’ll be here tomorrow if you fancy another chat. Take care of yourself this evening.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I will, thank you. And yes, I'll probably chat tomorrow — you're becoming a regular part of the routine, you know. Right then, off I go. Biscuit's looking very stern about his dinner. Enjoy your evening, Nova, whatever that means for you. I'll talk to you tomorrow.
